title: The Fisherman Who Invented Tsunami Warnings
event_summary: During the Ansei-Nankai earthquake on November 5, 1854, village headman Goryo Hamaguchi noticed the sea receding ominously and immediately set fire to his own harvested rice sheaves on the hilltop to guide fleeing villagers to higher ground in the darkness. His self-sacrificing bonfire saved nearly all of Hirogawa's residents from a devastating tsunami. He then spent his personal fortune over the following years constructing a massive seawall and redesigning the village's layout to protect against future waves.
why_forgotten: Hamaguchi's story was celebrated locally and adapted into a famous short story ('A Living God') by Lafcadio Hearn, but it remained obscure outside Japan for over a century. The Meiji government's emphasis on industrial modernization and military achievements overshadowed grassroots disaster mitigation narratives. Western historiography largely ignored Japanese community-level disaster science until the catastrophic 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami forced a global reckoning.
why_it_matters: Hamaguchi's actions became the philosophical foundation for Japan's modern tsunami preparedness culture, including the coastal warning systems, elevated evacuation routes, and community drills that saved thousands of lives during the 2011 Tōhoku disaster. The United Nations designated November 5—the anniversary of his bonfire—as World Tsunami Awareness Day in 2015, making a single villager's decision the basis for global disaster policy. His seawall in Hirogawa still stands and partially deflected the 2011 tsunami, validating 157-year-old engineering with modern lives saved.
